domain_label: Study System — Learner Model & Adaptivity: Knowledge Tracing (single user)
purpose: A method for estimating, per concept-tag, what a single learner knows from their own answer stream — BKT's four-parameter HMM with its correct/incorrect posterior and learning-transition equations, DKT noted as the population-scale option not to build, Elo/Glicko-style dual rating of learner ability and item difficulty, and IRT (3PL/2PL/Rasch) as the conceptual frame — kept honest by carrying each formula as published, tagging every claim FACT/ESTIMATE/UNKNOWN, and refusing to hard-code the egress-blocked Glicko update equations.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every model-selection call is an ESTIMATE synthesized from the cited literature
the system serves a SINGLE user, which rules out any model that needs a population of learners (DKT) and makes cheap online estimators (BKT, Elo) the practical set

published formulas are transcribed as retrieved through WebSearch; where a step rests only on prior knowledge it is tagged ESTIMATE, and the canonical Glicko update equations are held UNKNOWN because glicko.net was egress-blocked (proxy 403) in the grounding session
the per-CARD memory/forgetting model (FSRS DSR) is treated as an already-built neighboring layer this KB depends on but does not re-derive
exclusions: the FSRS DSR memory-model formulas, revlog schema and optimizer (neighboring KB spaced_repetition_and_anki.md) beyond naming FSRS as the separate scheduling layer BKT's no-forgetting assumption requires

the weakness-diagnosis error taxonomy (slip/misconception/missing-prerequisite/retrieval-failure), differential-diagnosis probes and confusion-matrix bookkeeping (neighboring learner KB) beyond emitting the uncertainty-gated probe trigger
the desirable-difficulties evidence and the ~85% success-rate challenge-calibration target (neighboring learner KB) beyond feeding the estimated mastery into item selection
the full nightly-analysis pipeline (ingest, retention calibration, card-quality pass, schedule build, reporting) beyond the skill-model update and its sanity loop
training or serving DKT/deep models, which are recorded as population-scale-only and explicitly not built for one user

competency_questions.question: What are the four BKT parameters and the HMM structure that estimates whether a single learner knows one skill?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names P(L0), P(T), P(G), P(S), the binary latent known/not-known state, the guess/slip emission channel and the no-forgetting assumption, with the Corbett & Anderson 1995 / van de Sande citation

competency_questions.question: What are the BKT posterior update equations after a correct and after an incorrect answer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives P(L|correct)=P(L)(1-P(S))/[P(L)(1-P(S))+(1-P(L))P(G)] and P(L|wrong)=P(L)P(S)/[P(L)P(S)+(1-P(L))(1-P(G))] as Bayes' rule with guess/slip likelihoods, tagged FACT

competency_questions.question: How is the predicted probability of a correct next response computed in BKT?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states P(correct)=P(L)(1-P(S))+(1-P(L))P(G) is exactly the denominator of the correct-answer posterior, and is the quantity compared to the observed answer for calibration

competency_questions.question: How does BKT apply learning across an opportunity, and why is a separate FSRS memory model still required?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives P(L_next)=P(L|obs)+(1-P(L|obs))P(T), states the no-forgetting property makes P(L) monotonic non-decreasing, and concludes a separate forgetting model (FSRS) handles scheduling

competency_questions.question: How are the BKT parameters fit and what guards degenerate fits?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names EM / Baum-Welch (forward-backward) on response sequences as FACT and the P(G)<0.3, P(S)<~0.1-0.3 degeneracy caps as high-confidence ESTIMATE, with the single-user nightly-batch, data-gated framing

competency_questions.question: How does Elo rate both the learner and the item, and what are its expectation and update formulas?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives p=1/(1+e^-(theta-d)), theta<-theta+K(y-p), d<-d-K(y-p), K=0.4 as a used value, the match-between-student-and-item framing (Pelanek 2016) and the O(1) per-answer property

competency_questions.question: What does Glicko's rating deviation add, and why are its exact update equations held UNKNOWN here?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states RD makes ratings distributions not points, grows in inactivity and shrinks with play, and that the canonical Glicko update equations are UNKNOWN because glicko.net was egress-blocked and must not be hard-coded before fetching glicko.pdf

competency_questions.question: How does the item side of Elo surface miscalibrated cards?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains that a card whose Elo difficulty drifts far from its concept-siblings is a card-quality flag routed to the flashcard specialist, using the same rating machinery that finds weak concepts

competency_questions.question: What is the IRT 3PL model and how do 2PL and 1PL/Rasch nest under it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives P(correct|theta)=c+(1-c)/(1+e^-a(theta-b)) with theta/b/a/c defined, states 2PL sets c=0 and 1PL/Rasch fixes a common a, and notes full calibration needs many respondents so IRT is the frame not the estimator

competency_questions.question: Why is educational Elo best understood as online Rasch estimation?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states the Elo expectation 1/(1+e^-(theta-d)) is exactly the Rasch/1PL curve so Elo is a streaming approximation of Rasch, citing the IRT-vs-BKT relation paper

competency_questions.question: Why should a correct MCQ move mastery estimates less than a correct free-recall answer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ties the IRT guessing floor c (~0.25 for a 4-option MCQ) to weighting MCQ correct answers as weaker mastery evidence than typed/spoken free recall

competency_questions.question: Which model runs at which layer for a single user, and why is DKT not built?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: maps FSRS (memory, per card), BKT (skill, per concept), Elo+RD (challenge-matching), IRT guessing-floor (format) to their cadences and records DKT as population-scale-only with its AUC-0.85-vs-0.68 result and thousands-of-learners requirement

competency_questions.question: How does per-concept uncertainty decide when a weakness is real enough to probe?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states a concept is probed when mastery is low AND uncertainty is low (a confident weakness), while high uncertainty means gather one or two more observations first, keeping diagnosis from thrashing on noise

competency_questions.question: What is the nightly skill-model update, its self-check loop, and the recommended single-user stack?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes the idempotent nightly replay through BKT and Elo with upward uncertainty decay for untouched concepts, the degeneracy/divergence freeze-and-fallback sanity loop, and the go verdict (BKT starter + Elo dual rating + IRT frame + MCQ weighting, no DKT, no hard-coded Glicko)

glossary.definition: Corbett & Anderson (1995) model of a single skill as a latent binary state (known/not-known) in a four-parameter Hidden Markov Model — P(L0) initial mastery, P(T) learn transition, P(G) guess, P(S) slip — updated by Bayes' rule after each correct/incorrect observation; the interpretable, low-data starter skill model.

The BKT emission parameters: P(S)=prob of a WRONG answer while the skill IS known (a slip); P(G)=prob of a CORRECT answer while the skill is NOT known (a guess). They are why a single wrong answer does not collapse the mastery posterior and why a single correct MCQ is weak evidence.

The classic-BKT constraint P(known->unknown)=0, which makes the mastery posterior monotonic non-decreasing; because real memory decays, a separate forgetting/memory model (FSRS DSR) is required for review scheduling, so BKT estimates mastery while FSRS estimates recall.

Piech et al. (2015) LSTM/RNN over (question-id, correct?) tuples emitting a per-step mastery vector; AUC 0.85 vs 0.68 for standard BKT on Khan Academy but uninterpretable and needing thousands of learners, so it is recorded as the population-scale option and NOT built for a single user.

Pelanek (2016) use of the Elo system in education: each answer is a 'match' between a learner ability theta (per concept) and an item difficulty d, with expectation p=1/(1+e^-(theta-d)) and O(1) updates theta<-theta+K(y-p), d<-d-K(y-p); the same machinery rates the learner's weak concepts and every card's difficulty at once.

Glickman (1995) extension of Elo giving each rating an explicit uncertainty (a distribution, not a point): low-RD estimates move less per result, RD grows during inactivity and shrinks with play; used here as an RD-like per-concept uncertainty scalar because the exact Glicko update equations are UNKNOWN (glicko.net egress-blocked).

Item Response Theory three-parameter logistic curve P(correct|theta)=c+(1-c)/(1+e^-a(theta-b)) with theta ability, b difficulty, a discrimination (slope), c pseudo-guessing lower asymptote (~0.25 for a 4-option MCQ); 2PL sets c=0, 1PL/Rasch also fixes a common a leaving only per-item b.

The observation that the educational-Elo expectation 1/(1+e^-(theta-d)) IS the Rasch/1PL curve, so Elo is a streaming, O(1) approximation of Rasch/IRT estimation — the bridge that lets a single-user system use cheap Elo updates while borrowing IRT's ability-vs-difficulty-vs-guessing interpretation.

The c lower asymptote of MCQ items: because ~25% of 4-option 'correct' answers are chance, a correct MCQ carries weaker mastery evidence than a correct typed/spoken free-recall answer, so skill-model updates are weighted by question format.

The batch step that replays the day's answers through BKT and Elo and decays per-concept uncertainty upward for untouched concepts, written to be order-safe and re-runnable (crash then rerun yields the same state) over an append-only answer log, never mutating history in place.

nodes.definition: Frame the single-user knowledge-tracing problem: estimate, per concept-tag (skill), the latent probability the one learner knows that skill from their own answer stream. Knowledge tracing is a per-SKILL layer sitting ON TOP of the per-CARD memory model (FSRS DSR, handled by a neighboring KB): the memory model says WHEN a specific card is due, the skill model says WHETHER the underlying concept is mastered. Four model families exist in ascending data hunger — BKT (Corbett & Anderson 1995), DKT (Piech et al. 2015), Elo/Glicko ratings (Pelanek 2016), IRT — and for a single user the practical set is BKT plus Elo with IRT as the conceptual frame [FACT for the family roster and citations per the research file; ESTIMATE for the single-user selection].

included: the per-concept single-user estimation goal
the skill-layer-on-top-of-FSRS-memory-layer split
the four-family roster in ascending data hunger

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a memory-model contract change or a move beyond single-user revises the frame

pros.claim: Framing knowledge tracing as a per-concept layer above the per-card memory model keeps mastery estimation and review scheduling from being conflated
pros.example: answering 'does the learner know periodontal anatomy' with a skill model while FSRS separately answers 'when is card 412 due'

cons.claim: The four-family framing is a literature synthesis, not a measured comparison on this user, so the practical-set choice is a judgment that data could revise
cons.example: assuming BKT+Elo is right before any calibration data exists to confirm it beats a simpler heuristic

failure_modes: collapsing the skill model into the memory model so mastery and recall are confused
picking a population-scale model without noticing the single-user data limit
acceptance_tests: the framing states the per-concept estimation goal, the skill-vs-memory split, and the four-family roster with citations and the single-user selection tagged ESTIMATE
revisit_triggers: a neighboring KB changes the memory-model contract
the system moves beyond a single user
calibration data contradicts the practical-set choice

nodes.definition: Fix the representation of what is being estimated, because it drives every update rule downstream. BKT models mastery as a latent BINARY state (known/not-known) inside a Hidden Markov Model; IRT and Elo model it as a CONTINUOUS ability theta on a logistic scale against an item difficulty. These are two views of 'does the learner know it': a probability P(L) that a binary latent is in the known state, versus a real-valued ability. The binary-state view yields Bayesian posterior updates (BKT); the continuous-ability view yields additive rating updates (Elo) and item-characteristic curves (IRT) [FACT — HMM binary latent for BKT and continuous theta for IRT/Elo per the cited sources].

included: the binary-latent (BKT) vs continuous-ability (Elo/IRT) representations
how each representation implies its update style
excluded: the specific posterior and rating equations

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new representation or a divergence between the two estimates changes the choice

pros.claim: Deciding the representation first prevents mixing a binary posterior update with an additive rating update by accident
pros.example: knowing a BKT node holds a probability P(L) while an Elo node holds a real-valued theta before either update is coded

cons.claim: The two representations are not interchangeable, so a system that needs both must maintain and reconcile two mastery estimates per concept
cons.example: a concept simultaneously carrying P(L)=0.7 from BKT and theta well above d from Elo that must be read together

failure_modes: applying a rating-style additive update to a binary probability
treating theta and P(L) as the same quantity
acceptance_tests: the representation names binary-latent BKT and continuous-ability Elo/IRT and links each to its update style
revisit_triggers: a third representation is introduced
the two estimates diverge and must be reconciled
the model-selection map changes which representation leads

nodes.definition: Define the four BKT parameters per skill (Corbett & Anderson 1995; van de Sande, JEDM; Baker et al.): P(L0) initial mastery (prob known before any practice), P(T) transition/learn probability (prob an unknown skill becomes known between opportunities), P(G) guess (prob of a correct answer when NOT known), P(S) slip (prob of a wrong answer when known). Knowledge is a binary latent in a Hidden Markov Model; observations (correct/incorrect) are emitted through the guess/slip channel. Classic BKT assumes no forgetting, i.e. P(known->unknown)=0 [FACT — four-parameter HMM structure per https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1115329.pdf and the Baker behaviormetrika paper]. Four parameters per concept-tag work from the first handful of answers and stay fully interpretable.

included: the definitions of P(L0), P(T), P(G), P(S)
the binary-latent HMM with a guess/slip emission channel
the no-forgetting assumption

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a BKT extension or a degenerate fit changes the parameter set

pros.claim: Four interpretable parameters per concept let a single user's mastery be stated as a readable probability from the first answers
pros.example: reporting 'P(knows periodontal-anatomy)=0.72' after only a handful of interactions

cons.claim: Only four parameters cannot capture forgetting or item-specific difficulty, so BKT alone under-models real memory and item variation
cons.example: a concept marked mastered by BKT that the learner has actually forgotten because no-forgetting is assumed

failure_modes: swapping the meaning of guess and slip
assuming BKT captures forgetting when it structurally does not
acceptance_tests: the four parameters are defined with the correct guess/slip semantics, the binary-latent HMM and emission channel are stated, and the no-forgetting assumption is named with the citation
revisit_triggers: a per-item or forgetting extension of BKT is adopted
a degenerate fit reveals a mis-specified parameter
the concept-tag granularity changes

nodes.definition: Give the Bayesian posterior on the latent mastery after one observation, the core BKT update. After a CORRECT answer: P(L|correct) = P(L)*(1-P(S)) / [ P(L)*(1-P(S)) + (1-P(L))*P(G) ]. After an INCORRECT answer: P(L|wrong) = P(L)*P(S) / [ P(L)*P(S) + (1-P(L))*(1-P(G)) ]. Each is Bayes' rule with the guess/slip emission likelihoods: a correct answer is evidence of mastery discounted by the guess rate, a wrong answer is evidence against mastery discounted by the slip rate [FACT — update equations as retrieved from the cited BKT sources]. This is the equation the nightly job replays per answer; misplacing P(S) vs P(G) silently inverts the evidence, so its direction must be unit-tested.

included: the correct-answer posterior equation
the incorrect-answer posterior equation
the Bayes'-rule-with-guess/slip interpretation

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a direction-test failure or a guess/slip re-fit changes the update

pros.claim: A closed-form Bayesian posterior updates mastery exactly per answer at negligible cost, ideal for a single-user nightly replay
pros.example: raising P(L) from 0.5 toward 1 on a correct answer and lowering it on a wrong one via two arithmetic expressions

cons.claim: The update is only as good as the guess/slip parameters, and swapping them inverts the evidence with no runtime error
cons.example: coding P(G) where P(S) belongs so a correct answer wrongly lowers the mastery estimate

failure_modes: placing P(S) and P(G) in the wrong branch and inverting the evidence
forgetting to feed the posterior into the learning transition before the next observation
acceptance_tests: both posterior equations are stated exactly, are identified as Bayes' rule with guess/slip likelihoods, and a direction test confirms correct raises and wrong lowers the posterior
revisit_triggers: a posterior direction test fails
the guess/slip parameters are re-fit
a per-item likelihood replaces the shared guess/slip channel

nodes.definition: State the predicted probability of a correct next response, which is exactly the DENOMINATOR of the correct-answer posterior: P(correct) = P(L)*(1-P(S)) + (1-P(L))*P(G). It is the probability of observing a correct answer given current mastery, mixing the known-and-not-slipping path with the unknown-but-guessing path [FACT — by definition of the HMM emission the cited sources describe]. This is the quantity to compare against the observed answer for calibration and AUC, and to feed challenge-matching (select items whose predicted correctness sits near a target success rate).

included: the P(correct) formula as the posterior denominator
its use for calibration/AUC and challenge-matching

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a calibration-metric or challenge-target change updates the prediction use

pros.claim: Reusing the posterior denominator as the prediction means calibration and challenge-matching cost nothing extra
pros.example: logging P(correct) each answer to build a predicted-vs-actual calibration curve for free

cons.claim: P(correct) inherits the guess floor, so on easy-to-guess items it stays high even when mastery is uncertain
cons.example: a high P(correct) driven by P(G) on a multiple-choice item masking a low P(L)

failure_modes: confusing P(correct) with the mastery posterior P(L)
calibrating against P(L) instead of P(correct)
acceptance_tests: P(correct) is given as the correct-answer posterior denominator and identified as the calibration and challenge-matching quantity
revisit_triggers: the calibration metric changes
the challenge-matching target is retuned
a per-item guess rate changes the prediction

nodes.definition: Apply the learning transition AFTER the evidence update: P(L_next) = P(L|obs) + (1-P(L|obs))*P(T) — the skill can be learned across the opportunity with probability P(T), so mastery not yet certain rises by the learn rate applied to the not-yet-known mass. Because classic BKT sets forgetting to zero, P(L) is monotonic non-decreasing, which is WHY a separate memory/forgetting model (FSRS) is still required for review scheduling [ESTIMATE, high confidence — canonical BKT transition step, consistent with the cited HMM but not verbatim in the retrieved text; the no-forgetting property itself is FACT]. Skill mastery (BKT) and recall probability (FSRS) are therefore distinct estimates the system keeps side by side.

included: the P(L_next) learning-transition equation
the no-forgetting monotonicity property
the consequent need for a separate FSRS memory model
excluded: forgetting-augmented BKT variants beyond naming them

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a forgetting extension or a BKT-vs-FSRS divergence changes the transition handling

pros.claim: Separating the learn transition from the evidence update keeps the two BKT effects (observing vs learning) explicit and orderable
pros.example: applying the correct-answer posterior first, then nudging upward by P(T) for the learning that occurred

cons.claim: The no-forgetting monotonicity is unrealistic for scheduling, forcing a second model and the risk of the two disagreeing
cons.example: BKT holding a skill at high mastery while FSRS shows recall has decayed and the card is overdue

failure_modes: using the no-forgetting BKT mastery to schedule reviews and missing decayed cards
applying the transition before the evidence update
acceptance_tests: the P(L_next) equation is stated, the no-forgetting monotonicity is identified as FACT with the transition step tagged ESTIMATE, and the separate-FSRS-for-scheduling conclusion is drawn
revisit_triggers: a forgetting-augmented BKT is adopted
BKT mastery and FSRS recall diverge materially
the transition/evidence ordering is questioned

nodes.definition: Fit the four parameters from response sequences by EM / Baum-Welch (forward-backward) [FACT — https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1115329.pdf], and guard degenerate fits: constrain P(G) < 0.3 and P(S) < ~0.1-0.3, otherwise the model 'explains' performance as guessing/slipping instead of knowledge and mastery becomes meaningless [ESTIMATE, high confidence — standard BKT practice]. For a single user, fitting is a nightly batch over the accumulated answer log; thin data yields unstable fits, so a refit is gated on enough observations (order of ~1000 total) and enough elapsed time, and otherwise skipped to avoid noise-driven parameter churn.

included: EM / Baum-Welch fitting on response sequences
the P(G)<0.3 and P(S)<~0.1-0.3 degeneracy caps
the data-and-time-gated single-user refit policy
excluded: the sanity/fallback loop that consumes the fit

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a refit gate crossing or a post-fit calibration drop changes the fitting policy

pros.claim: EM fitting with degeneracy caps produces stable, interpretable parameters instead of a model that hides knowledge behind guessing
pros.example: rejecting a fit that sets P(G)=0.5 because it would explain every correct answer as a lucky guess

cons.claim: EM on thin single-user data is unstable and can overfit, so refitting too often adds noise rather than signal
cons.example: a nightly refit on a few dozen new answers swinging P(T) wildly between days

failure_modes: refitting on thin data and churning the parameters
accepting a degenerate fit that maxes guessing or slipping
acceptance_tests: EM / Baum-Welch is named as FACT, the P(G) and P(S) degeneracy caps are stated as high-confidence ESTIMATE, and the refit is shown gated on data volume and elapsed time
revisit_triggers: accumulated data crosses the refit gate
a fit hits a degeneracy cap
calibration degrades after a fit

nodes.definition: Record DKT as the population-scale option, explicitly not to build here. Piech et al. 2015: an LSTM/RNN consumes the sequence of (question-id, correct?) tuples and outputs, at each step, a per-step mastery vector over all concepts; on the Khan Academy dataset it reached AUC 0.85 vs 0.68 for standard BKT (marginal baseline 0.63), with ~25-30% relative AUC gains across canonical datasets [FACT]. But much of that edge disappears once BKT is extended with forgetting/abilities (Khajah et al. 2016, 'How Deep is Knowledge Tracing?'), and DKT is uninterpretable and needs thousands of learners' data [ESTIMATE, high confidence — widely replicated critique]. For a single-user system it is NOT applicable: note it as the option that arrives only with a population, do not build it.

included: the DKT LSTM-over-(qid,correct) architecture and its AUC-0.85-vs-0.68 result
the disappearing-edge and uninterpretability/thousands-of-learners critique
the not-applicable-for-single-user verdict

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population of learners or an interpretable deep-KT variant changes the verdict

pros.claim: Recording DKT's population-scale requirement prevents wasting effort on a model that cannot train on one user
pros.example: citing the thousands-of-learners requirement to decline building an LSTM knowledge tracer for a solo learner

cons.claim: DKT's higher headline AUC is a standing temptation that ignores its interpretability and data costs
cons.example: chasing the 0.85-vs-0.68 number without noting the edge shrinks against extended BKT and needs a population

failure_modes: attempting to train DKT on single-user data
citing DKT's AUC without its data and interpretability caveats
acceptance_tests: the DKT architecture and AUC result are stated as FACT, the disappearing-edge/uninterpretable/thousands-of-learners critique is given, and the not-built-for-single-user verdict is recorded
revisit_triggers: a population of learners becomes available
an interpretable deep-KT variant matures
extended-BKT stops closing the AUC gap

nodes.definition: Define the Elo dual rating that rates the LEARNER and every ITEM at once (Pelanek 2016, 'Applications of the Elo rating system in adaptive educational systems,' Computers & Education 98:169-179): each answer is a 'match' between a learner skill theta (per concept) and an item difficulty d. Expected correctness: p = 1/(1+e^-(theta-d)). Update after observing y in {0,1}: theta <- theta + K*(y-p) and symmetrically d <- d - K*(y-p); K regulates step size and K = 0.4 has been considered appropriate in some educational settings [FACT — formula per the Elo-for-education literature, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.07028 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12784335/]. Updates are O(1) and work from the first interaction, making Elo the cheapest practical dual estimator for a single user.

included: the match-between-learner-and-item framing
the p=1/(1+e^-(theta-d)) expectation and the theta/d update rules
the O(1) per-answer, works-from-first-interaction property
excluded: the K decay policy (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a K retune, an RD extension, or a card-quality signal changes the dual rating

pros.claim: One O(1) update rates the learner's concept ability and the item's difficulty simultaneously, giving weak-concept detection and card-difficulty for the same cost
pros.example: a single correct answer nudging theta up and the item's d down in one pass

cons.claim: Point ratings carry no uncertainty, so an early or noisy result moves them as much as a well-observed one
cons.example: one lucky guess shifting a concept's theta far before enough evidence exists

failure_modes: updating theta without the symmetric d update, decoupling learner and item ratings
treating point ratings as certain and over-reacting to a single result
acceptance_tests: the expectation and both update equations are stated with K=0.4 as a used value, the match framing and Pelanek citation are given, and the O(1) property is noted
revisit_triggers: ratings thrash or lag and K must be retuned
an uncertainty extension (RD) is added
the item-side ratings surface card-quality issues

nodes.definition: Set the K step-size policy for the Elo update. K regulates how far each result moves ratings; a common refinement makes K DECAY with the number of attempts, e.g. K = a/(1+b*n), so early answers move ratings more and a well-observed rating stabilizes [ESTIMATE, medium-high confidence — Pelanek 2016 describes an 'uncertainty function' variant, abstract-level verification only]. This is the Elo analogue of shrinking uncertainty and the lever that trades responsiveness (large K, fast adaptation, noise sensitivity) against stability (small K, slow drift, robustness); it is tuned so ratings neither thrash on single answers nor lag real change.

included: K as the responsiveness-vs-stability step size
the K=a/(1+b*n) attempt-decay refinement
the tuning goal of neither thrashing nor lagging
excluded: the Glicko RD formalization of uncertainty

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a thrash/lag observation or an RD replacement changes the K policy

pros.claim: Decaying K lets early answers move ratings fast and later answers move them little, matching confidence to evidence without a full uncertainty model
pros.example: a new concept's theta swinging freely at first then settling as attempts accumulate

cons.claim: The decay is an approximation to real uncertainty and its a,b constants are unverified, so it can mis-time stabilization
cons.example: K decaying too fast and freezing a rating before enough evidence has arrived

failure_modes: fixing K too high and thrashing on noise
decaying K too fast and freezing an under-observed rating
acceptance_tests: K is described as the responsiveness-vs-stability step size, the K=a/(1+b*n) decay is given as a medium-high-confidence ESTIMATE, and the no-thrash-no-lag tuning goal is stated
revisit_triggers: ratings thrash or lag in practice
a real RD uncertainty replaces the K-decay heuristic
the a,b constants are re-tuned from data

nodes.definition: Add explicit uncertainty via Glicko's rating deviation RD (Glickman 1995): ratings become distributions, not points; low-RD (well-measured) estimates move less per result; RD GROWS during inactivity and SHRINKS with play [FACT — Glicko RD concept per the retrieved overviews]. The EXACT Glicko update equations are [UNKNOWN] in this build: the canonical spec at glicko.net was egress-blocked (proxy 403) in the grounding session, so they must NOT be hard-coded without first fetching http://www.glicko.net/glicko/glicko.pdf. Until then, use an RD-LIKE per-concept uncertainty scalar (grow it when the concept is untouched, shrink it on each answer) as the practical stand-in that gates probing and the K analogue, without claiming the Glicko math it approximates.

included: RD as an explicit per-rating uncertainty that grows in inactivity and shrinks with play
the UNKNOWN status of the exact Glicko update equations and the do-not-hard-code rule
the RD-like uncertainty-scalar stand-in
excluded: the exact Glicko or Glicko-2 equations (blocked)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: fetching glicko.pdf or a mis-timed probe changes the uncertainty model

pros.claim: An explicit uncertainty distinguishes a well-measured weakness from an under-sampled one, which point Elo cannot do
pros.example: holding a low-confidence theta with high RD so the system gathers more evidence before intervening

cons.claim: The exact Glicko equations are unavailable here, so only an approximate uncertainty scalar can be used until the spec is fetched
cons.example: an RD-like scalar that mimics grow-in-inactivity/shrink-with-play without Glicko's calibrated volatility math

failure_modes: hard-coding Glicko update equations from memory while they are UNKNOWN
omitting uncertainty and treating every rating as equally certain
acceptance_tests: RD is defined as an explicit uncertainty that grows in inactivity and shrinks with play, the exact equations are marked UNKNOWN with the glicko.net block and the do-not-hard-code/fetch-glicko.pdf rule, and the RD-like scalar stand-in is named
revisit_triggers: glicko.pdf is fetched and the real equations become available
the uncertainty scalar mis-times probing
a Glicko-2 volatility term is considered

nodes.definition: Exploit the item side of Elo: because every card/question carries its own difficulty rating d, the same machinery that finds weak concepts also finds MISCALIBRATED cards. A card whose Elo difficulty drifts far above (or below) its concept-tag siblings under otherwise similar answers is a card-quality flag — mislabelled answer key, ambiguous wording, or a wrong concept-tag — routed to the flashcard-quality specialist rather than being read as learner weakness [ESTIMATE — design synthesis; the item-rating mechanism is FACT from Pelanek 2016]. This turns the learner model into a content-quality sensor for free, and protects mastery estimates from being corrupted by bad items.

included: item difficulty d as a per-card rating
difficulty-drift-vs-siblings as a card-quality flag
routing flagged cards to the flashcard specialist instead of blaming the learner

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: recurring item outliers or a confirmed hard-not-defective card changes the flag logic

pros.claim: The item ratings expose bad cards at no extra cost, keeping learner mastery estimates clean
pros.example: flagging a card whose difficulty rating sits far above its siblings as ambiguous rather than marking the concept unmastered

cons.claim: A drifted item rating can be genuine difficulty rather than a defect, so the flag needs confirmation before rewrite
cons.example: a legitimately hard edge-case card flagged as miscalibrated when it is simply the hardest item in its group

failure_modes: reading a bad-card difficulty drift as learner weakness
auto-rewriting a card that is merely genuinely hard
acceptance_tests: item difficulty is described as a per-card rating, difficulty-drift-vs-siblings is named a card-quality flag, and flagged cards are routed to the flashcard specialist rather than punishing the learner
revisit_triggers: item-difficulty outliers recur for the same card
a flagged card is confirmed genuinely hard not defective
the sibling-comparison threshold is tuned

nodes.definition: State the IRT 3PL model as the conceptual frame: P(correct|theta) = c + (1-c)/(1+e^-a(theta-b)), with theta ability, b difficulty (the theta where the c-adjusted curve passes its midpoint; for c=0, P=0.5 at theta=b), a discrimination (slope of the item-characteristic curve), and c pseudo-guessing lower asymptote (for a 4-option MCQ chance is ~0.25, though estimated c often differs) [FACT — 3PL per https://www.cogn-iq.org/learn/theory/three-parameter-logistic-model/ and the other cited IRT expositions]. Full IRT calibration needs many respondents per item, so for one user IRT is the FRAME (ability vs item difficulty vs guessing floor), not the estimator — Elo supplies the practical online estimate.

included: the 3PL formula with theta/b/a/c defined
the ~0.25 MCQ guessing-floor interpretation of c
the frame-not-estimator role for a single user

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population calibration or a guessing-floor revision changes the frame

pros.claim: The 3PL frame separates ability, difficulty, discrimination and guessing so the single-user estimator can borrow the interpretation without the data
pros.example: reading an Elo theta-vs-d gap through the Rasch lens while knowing the guessing floor limits MCQ evidence

cons.claim: 3PL parameters are unidentifiable from one user's data, so treating it as an estimator here would overfit or fail
cons.example: trying to estimate per-item a and c for a solo learner with a handful of responses per item

failure_modes: attempting to calibrate 3PL parameters from single-user data
ignoring the guessing floor c when interpreting MCQ correctness
acceptance_tests: the 3PL formula is given with theta/b/a/c defined, the ~0.25 MCQ guessing floor is stated, and the frame-not-estimator role for one user is noted
revisit_triggers: a population enables real IRT calibration
the guessing-floor weighting is revised
the Rasch equivalence link is reconsidered

nodes.definition: Place the nested simplifications of IRT: 2PL sets c=0 (no guessing floor), leaving discrimination a and difficulty b; 1PL/Rasch additionally fixes a common discrimination a across all items, leaving only per-item difficulty b [FACT — nested by definition of the models]. Fewer free parameters means far less data to identify the model, which is exactly why the 1PL/Rasch view — one difficulty per item, one ability per learner — is the version that maps onto a single-user online estimator, whereas 2PL and 3PL demand the per-item discrimination and guessing data a solo learner cannot supply.

included: 2PL as 3PL with c=0
1PL/Rasch as 2PL with a common a
why fewer parameters suit single-user data

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population calibration or an equal-discrimination violation changes the nesting choice

pros.claim: Naming the nesting shows precisely which IRT variant is identifiable for one user and which are not
pros.example: choosing the Rasch view (per-item b, per-learner theta) because it needs no per-item a or c

cons.claim: Collapsing to Rasch assumes equal discrimination and no guessing, which is wrong for MCQ items whose guessing floor still matters
cons.example: a Rasch estimate ignoring that a 4-option MCQ has a ~0.25 floor the guessing-floor node must reintroduce

failure_modes: assuming Rasch's equal-discrimination holds for all item types
dropping the guessing floor because Rasch has no c
acceptance_tests: 2PL (c=0) and 1PL/Rasch (common a) are placed as nested simplifications of 3PL and the fewer-parameters-suit-single-user point is made
revisit_triggers: a population enables 2PL/3PL identification
the equal-discrimination assumption is violated
the guessing floor must be reintroduced on top of Rasch

nodes.definition: Establish the key bridge between the estimator and the frame: the educational-Elo expectation 1/(1+e^-(theta-d)) IS exactly the Rasch/1PL item-characteristic curve, so Elo is best understood as an ONLINE, STREAMING approximation of Rasch estimation (also the framing in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.05926, 'Learning meets Assessment: on the relation between IRT and BKT') [FACT — by inspection of the two formulas]. This justifies using cheap O(1) Elo updates as the practical single-user estimator while borrowing IRT's interpretation — theta as ability, d as item difficulty, and the guessing floor as a format caveat — so the system gets Rasch's meaning without Rasch's batch-calibration data cost.

included: the identity between the Elo expectation and the Rasch/1PL curve
Elo as a streaming approximation of Rasch
using the equivalence to borrow IRT interpretation cheaply
excluded: the 2PL/3PL parameters Elo does not estimate

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a richer online estimator or a 1PL-limit misread changes the bridge

pros.claim: The equivalence lets a single-user system use O(1) Elo updates yet interpret them with IRT's ability/difficulty vocabulary
pros.example: reporting a concept's theta relative to item d as a Rasch-style ability estimate updated live

cons.claim: Elo only approximates Rasch and estimates neither discrimination nor guessing, so the equivalence holds only at the 1PL level
cons.example: reading an Elo theta as a full 3PL ability and ignoring the discrimination and guessing the 1PL view drops

failure_modes: over-reading Elo as full IRT rather than 1PL/Rasch only
forgetting that Elo omits discrimination and guessing
acceptance_tests: the Elo expectation is shown identical to the Rasch/1PL curve, Elo is framed as online Rasch with the relation-paper citation, and the borrow-interpretation-cheaply consequence is drawn
revisit_triggers: a 2PL/3PL online estimator is adopted
the 1PL-only limit of Elo causes a misread
the guessing floor must be layered on the Rasch interpretation

nodes.definition: Turn the IRT guessing floor c into an update-weighting rule. On a 4-option MCQ, ~25% of 'correct' answers are expected by chance, so a correct MCQ carries WEAKER mastery evidence than a correct typed or spoken free-recall answer; weight the skill-model update (BKT posterior and Elo step) by question format accordingly [FACT for the ~25% chance floor and its format dependence; ESTIMATE for the exact weighting]. Concretely, a free-recall correct should move P(L)/theta more than an MCQ correct, and formats with a higher guessing floor should contribute proportionally less mastery evidence — the format constant is static per question type.

included: the ~25% 4-option MCQ chance floor
weighting BKT/Elo updates by question format
free-recall corrects moving estimates more than MCQ corrects

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a validated format weight or a new question format changes the weighting

pros.claim: Weighting by format stops easy-to-guess MCQ corrects from inflating mastery estimates
pros.example: a spoken free-recall correct raising P(L) more than a lucky 4-option MCQ correct on the same concept

cons.claim: The exact per-format weights are unverified, so the rule fixes the direction but not the magnitude
cons.example: knowing MCQ evidence should count less without a validated multiplier for how much less

failure_modes: counting an MCQ correct as full mastery evidence
inventing a precise format weight the research did not verify
acceptance_tests: the ~25% MCQ guessing floor is stated, format-weighted updates are prescribed with free-recall > MCQ, and the exact weights are flagged as unverified ESTIMATE
revisit_triggers: a validated per-format weight is obtained
a new question format enters the system
guessing-floor drift is observed for a format

nodes.definition: Lay out which model runs where for a single user [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the cited machinery]: memory / when-to-review = FSRS DSR (per card, every review); skill / does-user-know-concept = BKT per concept-tag (every answer plus a nightly re-fit); challenge-matching = Elo (theta per concept, d per item) with an RD-style uncertainty (every answer); format correction = IRT guessing-floor c by question format (static constants). DKT is recorded as the population-scale-only option not built here. Each layer has a distinct granularity and update cadence so the four compose without duplicating each other — FSRS schedules, BKT judges mastery, Elo matches challenge and audits items, IRT corrects for format.

included: the FSRS/BKT/Elo+RD/IRT layer-to-cadence map
DKT recorded as population-scale-only
the non-duplication of the four layers by granularity/cadence

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a layer model swap or a cross-layer disagreement changes the map

pros.claim: A per-layer map assigns each question (when, whether, how-hard, format) to the cheapest model that answers it without overlap
pros.example: letting FSRS own scheduling and BKT own mastery so neither is asked to do the other's job

cons.claim: Four coordinated models are more moving parts to keep consistent than one, and their estimates can disagree
cons.example: BKT mastery, Elo theta and FSRS recall pointing different ways on the same concept and needing reconciliation

failure_modes: duplicating a function across two layers
asking one model to cover another layer's question (e.g. BKT for scheduling)
acceptance_tests: the map assigns FSRS/BKT/Elo+RD/IRT to their layers and cadences, records DKT as population-scale-only, and shows the layers do not duplicate each other
revisit_triggers: a layer's model is swapped
two layers' estimates chronically disagree
a population makes DKT viable

nodes.definition: Use the RD-style per-concept uncertainty to decide WHEN a flagged weakness is real enough to act on versus merely under-sampled: probe a concept when its mastery estimate is LOW and its uncertainty is LOW (a confident weakness), rather than firing on a single noisy answer [ESTIMATE — design synthesis; the RD uncertainty concept is FACT]. High uncertainty means gather one or two more observations before intervening; low uncertainty with low theta / low P(L) means schedule a diagnostic probe. This gate keeps the downstream weakness-diagnosis layer (a neighboring KB) from thrashing on noise and spends scarce probe slots only on weaknesses the data actually supports.

included: the low-mastery-AND-low-uncertainty probe condition
gathering more evidence when uncertainty is high
protecting the diagnosis layer from noise
excluded: the weakness-diagnosis error taxonomy and probe design (neighboring KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the real RD or a probe mis-timing changes the trigger threshold

pros.claim: Gating probes on confident weaknesses spends limited diagnostic slots only where the data supports a real gap
pros.example: probing a concept with low theta and low RD while deferring one with low theta but high RD

cons.claim: Because the uncertainty is an RD-like approximation, the confidence threshold is itself a tunable heuristic that can mis-time probes
cons.example: a threshold that probes too early on a still-uncertain concept or too late on a confidently weak one

failure_modes: probing on a single noisy answer without checking uncertainty
never probing because the uncertainty threshold is set unreachably tight
acceptance_tests: the trigger fires only on low-mastery-and-low-uncertainty, defers to more evidence when uncertainty is high, and is shown to protect the diagnosis layer from noise
revisit_triggers: the real Glicko RD replaces the approximate uncertainty
probes chronically mis-time
the diagnosis layer changes its probe budget

nodes.definition: Define the nightly skill-model batch step: replay the day's answers through BKT (per-concept posterior then learning transition) and Elo (theta per concept, d per item), then decay the Glicko-style uncertainty UPWARD for concepts untouched more than N days [ESTIMATE — design synthesis, grounded in the cited update rules]. The step is idempotent and order-safe (crash then rerun yields the same skill state), reads the append-only answer log (including late-arriving graded voice answers), and writes skill estimates as data with no in-place mutation of history. It is the per-concept counterpart to the FSRS memory pass and feeds the probe trigger, the item-drift flag and the sanity loop.

included: the nightly replay through BKT and Elo
upward uncertainty decay for untouched concepts
the idempotent, append-only, no-history-mutation discipline
excluded: the full nightly analysis pipeline (retention calibration, scheduling, reporting)
the BKT re-fit gating (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a non-idempotency bug or a decay-rate mis-timing changes the batch design

pros.claim: An idempotent nightly replay recomputes all skill estimates safely and cheaply for a single user without corrupting history
pros.example: re-running the job after a crash and getting identical per-concept theta and P(L)

cons.claim: A nightly cadence means intra-day mastery is stale until the next run, and the uncertainty-decay rate N is a heuristic
cons.example: a concept practiced this morning not reflected in the skill estimate until tonight's batch

failure_modes: mutating history in place so a re-run cannot reproduce the state
skipping the upward uncertainty decay so stale concepts look confidently known
acceptance_tests: the step replays answers through BKT and Elo, decays uncertainty upward for untouched concepts, and is shown idempotent and append-only with no history mutation
revisit_triggers: the job proves non-idempotent under a crash
the decay rate N mis-times uncertainty growth
the update cadence changes

nodes.definition: Add the self-check feedback loop on the skill models: run the BKT parameter-degeneracy checks (the P(G), P(S) caps from fitting) and watch Elo theta/d divergence; if a fit is degenerate or a rating diverges, FREEZE it and fall back to the previous parameters rather than shipping a broken model [ESTIMATE — design synthesis; the degeneracy caps are cited practice]. Every skill-model metric carries a stored daily snapshot (a trend, not a point), a threshold, and a named automatic action or human-visible flag — a metric with no consumer is deleted. This is the loop that catches a bad nightly fit before it corrupts mastery estimates and item selection.

included: BKT degeneracy checks and Elo divergence watch
freeze-and-fall-back-to-previous-parameters on a bad fit
the snapshot/threshold/named-action contract per metric
excluded: the retention-calibration and card-quality loops (neighboring pipeline)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a missed bad fit or a mis-set freeze threshold changes the sanity loop

pros.claim: A freeze-and-fallback guard stops a degenerate nightly fit from silently corrupting mastery and item selection
pros.example: reverting to yesterday's parameters when a new fit trips the P(G) cap

cons.claim: Freezing on a tripped check can also hold onto stale parameters if the threshold is mis-set
cons.example: a too-sensitive divergence check freezing a fit that was actually improving

failure_modes: shipping a degenerate fit because no sanity check runs
freezing indefinitely on an over-sensitive threshold
acceptance_tests: the loop runs the BKT degeneracy checks and Elo divergence watch, freezes and falls back on a bad fit, and gives every metric a snapshot, threshold and named action
revisit_triggers: a bad fit slips past the checks
the freeze threshold proves mis-set
a new skill-model metric is added

nodes.definition: Compose the recommended single-user knowledge-tracing stack, the go/no-go the KB builds toward. Go: BKT per concept-tag as the interpretable starter skill model (four parameters, works from the first answers, 'P(knows periodontal-anatomy)=0.72'); Elo dual rating (theta per concept, d per item) as the O(1) challenge-matcher and card-quality sensor; IRT as the conceptual frame (Elo = online Rasch) with the MCQ guessing floor as a format weighting; an RD-style per-concept uncertainty gating probes; all updated in the idempotent nightly batch with a degeneracy/divergence freeze-and-fallback sanity loop. No-go: do NOT build DKT (population-scale, needs thousands of learners), and do NOT hard-code the Glicko update equations while they are UNKNOWN. A model earns a place only when it is interpretable, cheap enough to run per answer for one user, and self-checked.

included: the go stack (BKT + Elo dual rating + IRT frame + MCQ weighting + RD probe gate + nightly batch + sanity loop)
the no-go on DKT and on hard-coded Glicko equations
the interpretable/cheap/self-checked acceptance rule
excluded: the neighboring weakness-diagnosis and desirable-difficulties decisions

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a population, a fetched Glicko spec, or a persistently failing model changes the verdict

pros.claim: The merged verdict commits to the cheapest interpretable stack that fits one user and explicitly refuses the models that do not
pros.example: shipping BKT+Elo with an IRT-informed weighting while declining DKT and un-fetched Glicko math

cons.claim: A single recommended stack can under-serve a concept whose best model differs, and it defers the Glicko and DKT calls to future data
cons.example: a concept that would benefit from richer uncertainty waiting on the un-fetched Glicko spec

failure_modes: building DKT or hard-coding Glicko against the no-go
adopting a model that is not interpretable, cheap per answer, and self-checked
acceptance_tests: the verdict states the go stack (BKT + Elo dual rating + IRT frame + MCQ weighting + RD probe gate + nightly batch + sanity loop), the no-go on DKT and un-fetched Glicko, and the interpretable/cheap/self-checked acceptance rule
revisit_triggers: a population enables DKT
glicko.pdf is fetched and RD math becomes available
the sanity loop reports a persistently failing model

conflict_axes.name: binary_state_vs_continuous_ability
conflict_axes.description: BKT represents mastery as a binary latent updated by Bayes' rule while Elo/IRT represent it as a continuous ability, and the two views do not reduce to each other.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: run both with distinct jobs — BKT for interpretable mastery, Elo for challenge-matching and item audit — and read P(L) and theta together

conflict_axes.name: interpretability_vs_predictive_power
conflict_axes.description: BKT is fully interpretable but lower-AUC while DKT predicts better but is a black box needing a population.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: for a single user prefer interpretable BKT; DKT's edge shrinks against extended BKT and requires thousands of learners

conflict_axes.name: responsiveness_vs_stability
conflict_axes.description: A large Elo step (high K) adapts fast but thrashes on noise, while a small step or low RD is stable but slow to reflect real change.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: let uncertainty set the step — large moves while uncertain, small once well-measured — via K decay or RD

conflict_axes.name: probe_now_vs_gather_more_evidence
conflict_axes.description: Acting on a flagged weakness early risks chasing noise, while waiting for certainty delays remediation.
poles: probe on the first low signal
wait until the weakness is confidently measured
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: probe only when mastery is low AND uncertainty is low; otherwise gather one or two more observations first

conflict_axes.name: mcq_convenience_vs_evidence_strength
conflict_axes.description: MCQ items are easy to author and grade but their guessing floor makes a correct answer weak mastery evidence versus free recall.
poles: treat every correct as full evidence
discount MCQ correctness by its guessing floor
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: weight updates by format so free-recall corrects move estimates more than MCQ corrects

conflict_axes.name: refit_often_vs_thin_data_noise
conflict_axes.description: Refitting BKT parameters frequently tracks change but on thin single-user data it churns the parameters with noise.
poles: gate refits on enough data and time
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: gate refits on data volume (~1000 reviews) and elapsed time, and freeze/fall back if calibration degrades

conflict_axes.name: no_forgetting_skill_vs_memory_decay
conflict_axes.description: BKT's no-forgetting mastery keeps rising while real recall decays, so mastery and scheduling pull apart.
poles: use rising BKT mastery for scheduling
schedule on a separate decaying memory model
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep BKT for mastery and FSRS for recall/scheduling; never schedule reviews off the no-forgetting mastery

conflict_axes.name: model_complexity_vs_single_user_data
conflict_axes.description: Richer models (DKT, 2PL/3PL) predict more but demand data a single learner cannot supply.
poles: adopt the richer model for accuracy
stay within what one user's data identifies
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: cap complexity at what single-user data identifies — BKT and 1PL-level Elo — and defer richer models to a population

conflict_axes.name: hardcode_glicko_vs_wait_for_spec
conflict_axes.description: The Glicko RD idea is wanted now but its exact equations were egress-blocked, tempting a from-memory implementation.
poles: use an RD-like scalar until glicko.pdf is fetched
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: never hard-code the UNKNOWN Glicko math; use the approximate RD-like uncertainty scalar until the spec is fetched

edge_cases.description: A single wrong answer on an otherwise-correct concept is read as loss of mastery
edge_cases.trigger: one isolated error is treated as strong negative evidence
edge_cases.mitigation: let P(S) price the slip so the posterior moves less on one error than on two, and rule out slip before intervening

edge_cases.description: EM returns a degenerate BKT fit that explains performance as guessing or slipping
edge_cases.trigger: P(G) or P(S) drifts high enough to absorb real knowledge
edge_cases.mitigation: apply the P(G)<0.3 and P(S)<~0.1-0.3 caps and freeze/fall back to the previous parameters

edge_cases.description: The guess and slip terms are swapped in the posterior update, silently inverting the evidence
edge_cases.trigger: P(S) and P(G) are placed in the wrong branch with no runtime error
edge_cases.mitigation: unit-test the update direction so a correct answer raises and a wrong answer lowers the posterior before wiring the batch

edge_cases.description: A correct 4-option MCQ is counted as full mastery evidence
edge_cases.trigger: format is ignored when updating the skill models
edge_cases.mitigation: weight updates by format so an MCQ correct moves estimates less than a free-recall correct

edge_cases.description: The Glicko update equations are hard-coded from memory while they are UNKNOWN
edge_cases.trigger: an implementer fills in RD math without fetching the spec
edge_cases.mitigation: use the RD-like uncertainty scalar and defer real Glicko math until glicko.pdf is fetched and verified

edge_cases.description: A long-untouched concept keeps a confident stale mastery estimate
edge_cases.trigger: uncertainty is not grown for concepts not practiced in N days
edge_cases.mitigation: decay the RD-like uncertainty upward for untouched concepts so stale estimates lose confidence

edge_cases.description: DKT is attempted on a single user's data
edge_cases.trigger: the higher-AUC headline drives a deep-model build for one learner
edge_cases.mitigation: record DKT as population-scale-only and do not build it without thousands of learners

edge_cases.description: Elo ratings thrash on noise or lag behind real change

edge_cases.mitigation: tune the K=a/(1+b*n) decay so early answers dominate and settled ratings resist single-answer noise

edge_cases.mitigation: compare the card's Elo difficulty to its concept-siblings and flag an outlier as a card-quality issue, not a mastery gap

workflow.gate: P(L_next) is stated, no-forgetting monotonicity is named, and the separate-FSRS conclusion is drawn

workflow.action: Fit the parameters with EM and guard degeneracy
workflow.description: Fit by EM/Baum-Welch with P(G)/P(S) caps under a data- and time-gated refit policy
workflow.gate: EM is named FACT, the caps are stated as ESTIMATE, and the refit is gated on data volume and time

workflow.action: Stand up the Elo dual rating and K policy
workflow.description: Rate theta per concept and d per item with the expectation and update equations and a K-decay policy
workflow.gate: the expectation and both update equations are stated with K=0.4 and the O(1) property, plus the K=a/(1+b*n) decay

workflow.action: Add RD-style uncertainty from the Glicko concept
workflow.description: Define RD as explicit uncertainty and use an RD-like scalar because the exact equations are UNKNOWN
workflow.gate: RD is defined, the exact equations are marked UNKNOWN with the do-not-hard-code/fetch-glicko.pdf rule, and the scalar stand-in is named

workflow.action: Apply the IRT frame and the MCQ guessing-floor weighting
workflow.description: State the 3PL frame, the nested 2PL/1PL, the Elo=online-Rasch bridge, and format-weight MCQ evidence
workflow.gate: the 3PL/2PL/1PL frame, the Rasch equivalence, and the ~25% MCQ guessing-floor weighting are stated with tags

workflow.action: Compose the model-selection map, nightly batch and probe trigger
workflow.description: Assign models to layers, replay answers nightly through BKT and Elo, decay uncertainty, and gate probes
workflow.artifact: model map + nightly batch + probe trigger
workflow.gate: the layer map, the idempotent nightly replay with upward uncertainty decay, and the low-mastery-low-uncertainty probe gate are stated

workflow.action: Run the sanity loop and issue the single-user stack verdict
workflow.description: Guard fits with freeze-and-fallback and commit to BKT+Elo+IRT-frame, no DKT, no hard-coded Glicko
workflow.gate: the sanity loop and the go/no-go verdict (BKT+Elo+IRT frame + MCQ weighting + RD probe gate + nightly batch; no DKT; no un-fetched Glicko) are stated

priority_rationale: The problem frame and mastery representation come first because they decide whether every downstream update is a Bayesian posterior or an additive rating; the BKT four parameters, posterior update, prediction, learning transition and fitting come next as the core interpretable skill model, with DKT recorded alongside as the population-scale option not built; the Elo dual rating, K policy, RD uncertainty and item-drift flag then supply the O(1) challenge-matcher and card-quality sensor; the IRT 3PL, nested models, Elo=online-Rasch bridge and MCQ guessing floor supply the conceptual frame and format weighting; and the model-selection map, uncertainty probe trigger, nightly batch, sanity loop and stack verdict come last because they compose every upstream estimator into an idempotent, self-checked single-user stack with an explicit no-go on DKT and on hard-coded Glicko math.

dominance_rules.rule: For a single user, the interpretable low-data model dominates the higher-AUC deep model
dominance_rules.rationale: DKT's AUC edge shrinks against extended BKT and it needs thousands of learners, while BKT is interpretable and works from the first answers
dominance_rules.trigger: a deep knowledge tracer is proposed for one learner
dominance_rules.action: use BKT per concept-tag and record DKT as the population-scale-only option not built

dominance_rules.rule: The FSRS memory model dominates BKT mastery for review scheduling
dominance_rules.rationale: classic BKT assumes no forgetting so its mastery posterior only rises, which cannot time reviews
dominance_rules.trigger: BKT mastery is about to drive scheduling
dominance_rules.action: schedule on FSRS recall and keep BKT strictly for mastery estimation

dominance_rules.rule: Free-recall evidence dominates MCQ evidence in skill updates
dominance_rules.rationale: a 4-option MCQ has a ~25% guessing floor so a correct MCQ is weaker mastery evidence than a correct free recall
dominance_rules.trigger: a correct answer updates the skill models
dominance_rules.action: weight the update by format so free-recall corrects move estimates more than MCQ corrects

dominance_rules.rule: A confident weakness dominates a single noisy answer for probing
dominance_rules.rationale: acting on one noisy result wastes scarce probe slots and thrashes the diagnosis layer
dominance_rules.action: probe only when mastery is low AND uncertainty is low; otherwise gather more evidence first

dominance_rules.rule: The previous good parameters dominate a degenerate or diverged new fit
dominance_rules.rationale: shipping a broken nightly fit corrupts mastery estimates and item selection
dominance_rules.trigger: a fit trips a degeneracy cap or an Elo divergence check
dominance_rules.action: freeze it and fall back to the previous parameters

dominance_rules.rule: The RD-like uncertainty stand-in dominates hard-coded Glicko equations while they are UNKNOWN
dominance_rules.rationale: the canonical Glicko spec was egress-blocked, so from-memory equations are unverifiable
dominance_rules.trigger: RD update math is about to be implemented
dominance_rules.action: use the approximate RD-like scalar and defer real Glicko math until glicko.pdf is fetched

dominance_rules.rule: Idempotent append-only replay dominates in-place mutation in the nightly job
dominance_rules.rationale: a non-idempotent job cannot recover from a crash and can corrupt history
dominance_rules.trigger: the nightly skill update writes state
dominance_rules.action: replay an append-only answer log and write estimates as data, never mutating history

dominance_rules.rule: The P(S)/P(G) degeneracy caps dominate the raw EM fit
dominance_rules.rationale: an unconstrained fit can explain knowledge away as guessing or slipping
dominance_rules.trigger: EM proposes parameters near the guessing/slipping extremes
dominance_rules.action: enforce P(G)<0.3 and P(S)<~0.1-0.3 and reject fits that violate them

dominance_rules.rule: An item-difficulty-drift card-quality flag dominates blaming the learner
dominance_rules.rationale: a bad item lowers observed correctness on its concept and would masquerade as a mastery gap
dominance_rules.trigger: a card's Elo difficulty drifts far from its concept-siblings
dominance_rules.action: flag the card to the flashcard specialist rather than marking the concept unmastered

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the binary-latent vs continuous-ability representation before writing any update rule
anti_rework_rules.prevents: coding a rating-style additive update onto a binary probability and reworking every update

anti_rework_rules.rule: Unit-test the posterior direction before wiring the nightly replay
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a swapped guess/slip inverting the evidence across the whole answer history

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide the model-per-layer map (FSRS/BKT/Elo/IRT) before coding
anti_rework_rules.prevents: two layers duplicating a function and being torn apart later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the MCQ format weighting before accumulating answers
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retroactively re-weighting a history of over-counted MCQ corrects

anti_rework_rules.rule: Gate BKT refits on enough data and time before scheduling nightly refits
anti_rework_rules.prevents: noise-driven parameter churn that has to be rolled back

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fetch the Glicko spec before hard-coding RD update equations
anti_rework_rules.prevents: implementing wrong equations from memory and ripping them out

anti_rework_rules.rule: Make the nightly job idempotent from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an un-replayable corrupted skill state after a mid-run crash

anti_rework_rules.rule: Add the P(G)/P(S) degeneracy caps when fitting is first implemented
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a degenerate model shipping and corrupting mastery before anyone checks

iteration_protocol.trigger: glicko.pdf is fetched and the canonical Glicko update equations become available
iteration_protocol.action: replace the RD-like uncertainty scalar with the real Glicko RD update and re-check the probe gate

iteration_protocol.trigger: accumulated reviews cross the refit gate (order of ~1000 total)
iteration_protocol.action: run the gated BKT re-fit and re-check the degeneracy caps

iteration_protocol.trigger: calibration (predicted vs actual correctness) degrades after a fit
iteration_protocol.action: revert to the previous parameters and record the regression

iteration_protocol.trigger: a population of learners ever becomes available
iteration_protocol.action: reconsider DKT and richer IRT/2PL/3PL against the single-user cap

iteration_protocol.trigger: a diagnosed weakness's fix chronically fails to recover mastery
item-difficulty outliers recur for the same cards
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the item-drift flag and route the cards for rewrite

iteration_protocol.trigger: Elo ratings thrash or lag in practice
iteration_protocol.action: retune the K-decay constants a and b
